analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for companies that pay their CEO over 50 times the median worker.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations now pay a flat 21% federal income tax no matter how lopsided their pay is. This bill would add a surcharge on top of that rate for companies whose highest-paid executive earns more than 50 times what the median worker makes. The surcharge climbs with the gap, reaching 5 extra percentage points above 500 to 1. It would apply only to large companies — those that file public pay disclosures with the Securities and Exchange Commission, plus private companies with at least $100 million in average annual gross receipts — and the Treasury would write rules to stop companies from dodging it by shifting employees to outside contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the direct beneficiary would be the Treasury, which would collect extra revenue from high-pay-gap corporations. Workers at those companies would benefit indirectly: the bill gives corporations a tax reason to narrow pay gaps by lifting median pay or trimming executive compensation, and the bill explicitly directs regulators to block the contractor workaround. Americans broadly gain from the revenue and from shrinking the tax burden they otherwise carry.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The Treasury and workers at big firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a penalty of 0.5 to 5 percentage points on top of the flat 21% corporate rate, scaled to how far the CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1, with the maximum 5-point increase for ratios above 500 to 1 [S2] [S3].

It uses the pay-ratio number companies already must report publicly under SEC rules, and extends the requirement to large private companies with at least $100 million in average annual gross receipts, so the tax targets large firms rather than small businesses [S3].
The bill directs the Treasury to write regulations preventing companies from gaming the ratio, including by using contractors instead of employees, which closes the most obvious avoidance route [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with extreme pay gaps between their highest-paid executive and their median worker would pay a higher corporate tax rate. Their shareholders would bear part of that through lower after-tax returns, and companies might pass some of it to consumers through prices. Companies facing the tax could also respond by narrowing pay ratios — trimming executive pay or raising worker pay — which is the point of the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big companies with huge CEO pay gaps

drawbacks.text: The penalty is modest — 0.5 to 5 percentage points on top of a 21% rate — so it pressures but does not force companies to narrow pay gaps, and it never directly changes anyone's paycheck [S3].
Corporate tax increases fall partly on shareholders, including retirement savers, and can be passed to consumers through higher prices, so the cost does not land only on highly paid executives.
The bill reaches only SEC-reporting companies and private companies above the $100 million receipts threshold, so pay gaps at smaller firms would be untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a nudge, not a fix: it uses the tax code to make extreme pay gaps expensive, which could push some companies to raise median wages or trim executive pay, and it raises revenue for the government. The honest cost is that the tax is partly borne by shareholders and consumers rather than executives themselves, the surcharge is small enough that many companies might simply pay it, and it leaves smaller firms out entirely. It is a well-targeted but modest tool aimed at a real problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Barbara Lee and 19 colleagues introduced the bill on March 17, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S3] [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
Twenty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps keep paying the flat 21% rate with no surcharge, and the Treasury collects nothing extra from them. Workers gained nothing from the bill's death, since it never directly changed pay in the first place.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were House Democrats and the record shows no Republican support; with the bill never reaching a vote, the split was reflected in sponsorship alone.

industries.industry: Large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps
industries.note: These companies — typically big public retailers, restaurant chains, and tech firms whose executives earn hundreds of times the median worker's pay — would face a 0.5 to 5 point tax surcharge. Their interest in keeping the flat 21% rate runs against the bill's goal of narrowing pay gaps.

The bill directs Treasury to prevent companies from lowering their ratio by replacing employees with contractors, which could complicate outsourcing arrangements these firms rely on; the effect is secondary to the main tax.
Private corporations with average annual gross receipts under $100 million are explicitly exempt, so small firms face no new tax while larger competitors face the surcharge.
